title: New dimensions in magnetism and superconductivity via 3D nanoprinting with focused electron and ion beams
authors: Claire Donnelly, Rosa Córdoba, Amalio Fernández-Pacheco
abstract: The extension of nanoscale quantum materials to the third dimension brings new possibilities to geometrically tune emergent properties, emulating or indeed going beyond the physics of bulk materials, with exciting implications for high-density technological integration. Realising such three-dimensional architectures requires nanofabrication techniques that not only enable complex 3D geometries, but also deliver functional quantum materials with emergent phenomena. Recent advances in focused electron- and ion-beam induced deposition (FEBID and FIBID) have made 3D nanopatterning of functional materials in complex geometries increasingly feasible, paving the way for the experimental realisation of new phenomena and device prototyping. In this review, we discuss the use of FEBID and FIBID 3D nanopatterning of superconducting and magnetic materials. We address the underlying mechanisms, and capabilities of these techniques, focusing on the physical phenomena that become accessible. Considering the resolution of the techniques in the context of the fundamental lengthscales of the materials, we discuss the emergent effects that arise due to three dimensional geometries in magnetic and superconducting nanostructures, and highlight perspectives for future developments of the techniques.
summary: This review surveys the use of 3D nanopatterning techniques, specifically FEBID and FIBID, to create complex nanostructures from superconducting and magnetic materials. It details how controlling the geometry—such as introducing chirality or curvature—allows researchers to access and study emergent physical phenomena that are inaccessible in bulk samples. The work highlights the potential of these methods for next-generation quantum device prototyping.
main_problem: The paper addresses the challenge of extending quantum materials into the third dimension (3D) to geometrically tune emergent properties beyond those found in bulk materials.
main_result: Focused electron and ion beam induced deposition (FEBID/FIBID) are powerful techniques enabling the realization of complex 3D nanostructures for studying emergent magnetic and superconducting phenomena.
method: The review discusses the capabilities and underlying mechanisms of 3D nanopatterning using FEBID and FIBID, which allow for direct writing of functional materials.
model_or_system: The physical systems studied are superconducting and magnetic materials patterned into complex 3D nanostructures, allowing control over chirality, curvature, and topology.
key_observables: Magnetization structures (e.g., domain walls, vortices), persistent currents, and superconducting screening currents.
important_parameters: The study operates in an intermediate regime between the superconducting coherence length ($\xi \sim 5-10 	ext{ nm}$) and the London penetration depth ($\lambda \sim 450-850 	ext{ nm}$); resolution is key, down to the few nanometers.
main_assumptions: The primary limitation noted is the experimental challenge of maintaining fidelity and achieving uniform properties in highly complex, sub-100 nm 3D geometries.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the variety of 3D nanostructure architectures achievable via FEBID/FIBID, including chiral, curved, and topologically non-trivial designs.
paper_structure: The review systematically discusses the necessity of 3D patterning, details the capabilities of FEBID/FIBID, and then analyzes the specific emergent effects observed in magnetic (e.g., domain walls) and superconducting (e.g., Meissner currents) nanostructures based on geometry.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer geometry at the nanoscale allows for the controlled study of topological and curvature-induced effects in quantum materials, which is highly relevant for understanding emergent quantum phenomena.
